definition: Discrepancy means a mismatch between things that should correspond — a gap that might still be explained or squared.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word discrepancy. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know discrepancy should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The moving company's invoice listed eleven boxes; Dana's photos showed nine - a discrepancy she circled twice in red.
Variation is the everyday wiggle between two honest readings; a discrepancy goes further - a gap wide enough to demand an explanation.
Contradiction outranks discrepancy: two figures with a discrepancy might yet be squared, but two accounts in contradiction can never both be true.

A mismatch is the plain word for two things failing to line up - socks, schedules, totals. A discrepancy is a mismatch with paperwork stakes: it sits between records that were supposed to correspond and demands an explanation before work can proceed. Every discrepancy is a mismatch; only the consequential ones earn the formal name.

An inconsistency is a failure to hold together across statements or behavior - Tuesday's story clashing with Friday's version. A discrepancy is narrower and more numerical: a measurable gap between two records of one fact. People and testimony show inconsistency; ledgers, invoices, and birth certificates show a discrepancy.

Some clerk, sixty years ago, had slipped by a day - and until the two records agreed, the application sat in a drawer.
Discrepancy is the precise word because two official records of one fact refuse to agree.
The word passes no judgment - it does not say which paper is wrong or accuse anyone of lying.
It just names the gap, and gaps in records must be explained before anything built on them can proceed.
A discrepancy lives between two records that should match and don't - ledgers, counts, clocks.
It is a fact to explain, not an accusation.
Keep it apart from ambiguity, this unit's two-readings word: ambiguity is one text read two ways; a discrepancy is two accounts of one fact.

Every ten years the museum counts its Roman coins.
The 1954 catalog lists sixty-three; this spring, the interns counting the trays reached sixty-one, twice.
A discrepancy of two coins is small in number and large in consequence, because the two records describe the same locked case and are supposed to agree exactly.
Coins had been reclassified before; a 1961 note mentioned two forgeries pulled for study and, perhaps, never logged back in.
But the registrar could not simply choose a number.
Until the gap was explained, the collection could not be insured, loaned, or exhibited.
It took a month in the archives to square the records — the forgeries, it turned out, had been in a basement drawer since Eisenhower.
